summary: The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) will eventually need to move to a new, probably stronger, set of cryptographic algorithms. This document describes the process that Certification Authorities and Relying Parties follow for that transition. It expects the change to take several years, so it does not define an emergency procedure, and it supports only a top-down migration in which parents move before children.

eli5.summary: Locks eventually need replacing with stronger ones. This explains the careful, slow order in which everyone swaps their locks so nothing breaks along the way.

questions: how to migrate rpki to new cryptographic algorithms
how does the rpki migrate to a new algorithm suite
what is the rpki twilight date
why is there no emergency rpki algorithm transition
subtitle: A phased, top-down plan for moving the RPKI from one cryptographic algorithm suite to the next without breaking routing security.

tldr.problem: The RPKI will eventually need a new, probably stronger, signature and hash algorithm suite, but thousands of independent CAs and Relying Parties cannot all switch at the same moment.
tldr.mechanism: A published timetable sets five milestones. CAs migrate parent before child and publish a parallel Suite B hierarchy next to Suite A, RPs move to Suite B in stages, and Suite A is deprecated at the end.
tldr.outcome: The process is meant to take several years and has no emergency path. It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 182), so a real transition needs its own timetable document.

today: RFC 6916 is a Best Current Practice and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. The algorithm suites themselves are defined elsewhere, in RFC 6485, which a real transition must update.

sections.title: Why Algorithms Need a Migration Plan
sections.content:
The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) already has a procedure for key rollover with the same algorithm suite, covered in RFC 6489. This document covers the harder case: a planned rollover because the signature algorithm suite changes. A suite is a signature algorithm (with a key size range) plus a one-way hash algorithm.

Every RPKI data structure names its algorithms, but the RFC says that is not enough. Protocols, infrastructure and operational procedures must also cope with the switch. Migration is expected to be very infrequent and to need a "current" and a "next" suite side by side for probably several years. Adopting a new hash algorithm while keeping the signature algorithm counts as a migration and requires the CA to change its key.

The document does not choose a new suite. RFC 6485 defines the required algorithms, and it MUST be updated when a transition starts. The certificate policy does not change, so the policy OID in RPKI certificates stays the same.
sections.eli5: Locks wear out, so one day everyone has to change them. This RFC is the instruction sheet for doing it slowly and safely, but it does not say which new lock to buy.

sections.title: Suites, Parents and Corresponding Objects
sections.content:
The RFC uses Algorithm Suite A for the current suite and Algorithm Suite B for the next one. In its examples, CA X is the parent of CA Y, a non-leaf CA, and CA Z is a child of CA Y. A leaf CA issues only end-entity (EE) certificates, while a non-leaf CA issues certificates to other CAs.

Two objects correspond when they say the same thing under different suites. Two certificates correspond if they go to the same entity from the same CA and bind identical Internet Number Resources. Two manifests correspond if they cover corresponding certificates, ROAs, CRLs and other signed objects. A signed product set is the certificates, signed objects, CRL and manifest that can be verified under the same parent CA certificate.
sections.eli5: Corresponding objects are like a document and its translation: written in a different language but saying exactly the same thing.

sections.title: Milestones and Phases
sections.content:
The first step is to update RFC 6485 to define Suite B and to publish an algorithm transition timetable as a BCP. Each date in it is one minute after midnight UTC. Five milestones divide the process into phases.

  • CA Ready Algorithm B Date (Phase 1): non-leaf CAs MUST be ready to handle a child's request for a Suite B certificate, and CAs publishing a Suite A Trust Anchor Locator MUST also publish a Suite B one.
  • CA Go Algorithm B Date (Phase 2): every CA MUST have reissued all its signed product sets under Suite B and keep them corresponding to Suite A.
  • RP Ready Algorithm B Date (Phase 3): all Relying Parties (RPs) MUST be able to process Suite B material.
  • Twilight Date (Phase 4): CAs MAY stop issuing under Suite A, and RPs MAY stop validating it. Suite B is now "current".
  • End-Of-Life Date: Suite A MUST be deprecated and its TALs removed, which returns the system to steady-state Phase 0. Suite B is then called Suite A.

CAs migrate top-down: CA Y issues under Suite B only after CA X has. A CA MUST NOT sign a CA certificate whose subject key belongs to a different suite, because a non-top-down approach would need such mixed certificates and lead to exponential growth of the RPKI repository.
sections.eli5: There are five checkpoints, like levels in a game. Teachers get ready first, then everyone starts using the new thing, and finally the old thing is retired.

sections.title: What Each Phase Asks of RPs and CAs
sections.content:
In Phase 1, the Suite B product tree is incomplete, so for production RPs MUST fetch and validate only Suite A products. Suite B is for testing, and Suite B products SHOULD sit at independent publication points so RPs are not affected.

In Phase 2, every product set exists under both suites. RPs MUST validate Suite A and MAY validate Suite B; it is RECOMMENDED that RPs able to process Suite B do so. If results differ, successful validation of either set is acceptable. In Phase 3, all RPs MUST validate Suite B, and SHOULD try the Suite B repository first, falling back to Suite A if needed. CA behavior does not change.

In Phase 4, all signed product sets MUST be issued under Suite B and MAY also be issued under Suite A. RPs MUST validate Suite B and SHOULD use only Suite B, because the Suite A collection may be incomplete.

Revocation follows the same logic. During Phases 2 and 3 a CA MUST revoke consistently under both suites. In Phase 1 a Suite A revocation SHOULD be mirrored to Suite B, and in Phase 4 the reverse.
sections.eli5: First only the teachers try the new way, then everybody tries it with the old way still available, and at the end the old way is put away.

sections.title: Finding Out Which Suites a Parent Supports
sections.content:
A child CA must learn which suites its parent supports and tell the parent which one to use. The RPKI provisioning protocol (RFC 6492) already handles this by using a different resource class for each suite.

To discover support, the child opens a provisioning session, performs a list command, and reads the issuer's certificate in each resource class. The suite of each class matches the SubjectPublicKeyInfo of that certificate. To request a specific suite in an issue or revoke command, the child names the matching resource class.

The parent checks proof of possession (PoP) of the private key. A request for a suite that matches no resource class fails PoP and is not carried out. This is also why a CA cannot get a Suite B certificate before its parent supports Suite B.
sections.eli5: Before ordering the new lock, a child asks the parent which locks it can make. If the child asks for a kind the parent cannot make, the answer is simply no.

sections.title: Pausing, Repositories and Deprecation
sections.content:
If the community is not ready for a phase, the timetable MUST be reissued with later dates. If serious concerns arise about Suite B, the transition ends, the timetable is republished, the algorithm document MUST be superseded and products roll back to Suite A. In Phase 4, CAs MUST NOT remove Suite A product sets if the transition is delayed or abandoned.

The two parallel hierarchies SHOULD have independent publication points, as structured by RFC 6481. Ordinary key rollover is done independently per suite and follows RFC 6489.

To deprecate a suite every CA MUST stop issuing certificates under it, stop producing signed products other than the CRL and manifest, revoke the EE and CA certificates it issued under it, and remove any TAL for it. CAs SHOULD delete the old products and keep a publication point with only the CRL and manifest at least until the CRL nextUpdate. Because CAs act asynchronously, transient inconsistencies are likely but should fail safe: objects under the deprecated suite are rejected.
sections.eli5: If the new locks turn out to be bad, everyone can go back to the old ones. When the old ones are finally retired, each person cleans up their own, in their own time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An algorithm transition should be very infrequent and needs wide community consensus. It may be triggered by weakening cryptographic strength. Because the procedure takes years, the RPKI stays vulnerable to that weakness meanwhile, for example to a downgrade attack.

The RFC offers no emergency mechanism, because the authors do not believe one is feasible given the very large number of CAs and RPs. A CA that does not finish migrating by the end of life of the old suite will have invalid signed products, and an RP that does not follow the process cannot validate Suite B products. Such failures could leave an incomplete view of routing information and degrade routing in the public Internet.
sections.eli5: Changing locks slowly means the old, weak lock stays on the door for a while. Anyone who forgets to switch gets locked out.

items.label: CA Ready Algorithm B Date
items.desc: Non-leaf CAs can issue Suite B; RPs use Suite A in production.

items.label: CA Go Algorithm B Date
items.desc: Every product set exists under both suites.

items.label: RP Ready Algorithm B Date
items.desc: All RPs MUST validate Suite B.

items.label: Twilight Date
items.desc: Suite B is required; Suite A is optional.

items.label: End-Of-Life Date
items.desc: Suite A is deprecated; Suite B becomes the new Suite A.
